rationale: The hypothesis posits that behavioral abnormalities (including ADHD/hyperactivity, aggressive behavior, and ASD) occur in approximately 70-80% of individuals with FBXO11-related intellectual developmental disorder with dysmorphic facies and behavioral abnormalities (IDDFBA) and serve as discriminating features separating it from quiet or hypoactive presentations. The initial discovery cohort by Gregor et al. (2018) documented behavioral abnormalities in 17/20 (85%) individuals, and a subsequent 21-patient series reported behavioral dysregulation in 62% (13/21). However, significant counter-evidence and phenotypic divergence exist: in a familial cohort of 12 affected Chinese individuals across 5 families (Pan et al., 2024), externalizing behavioral abnormalities like ADHD or aggression were not reported across the cohort, with psychiatric/behavioral manifestations limited to hallucinations in only 1/12 (8.3%) individuals. Furthermore, familial reports (Lee et al., 2020) describe individuals presenting solely with mild ID and subtle facial dysmorphism without prominent behavioral disturbances, and hypotonia is documented in up to 62% of cases, refuting the claim that FBXO11 patients can be reliably distinguished from quiet/hypoactive syndromic ID presentations based on behavioral phenotypes alone.

evidence.text: In the initial cohort defining IDDFBA, behavioral problems were identified in 17 of 20 individuals harboring de novo FBXO11 variants, alongside autistic features, attention deficits, and variable intellectual disability.

source.title: De novo variants in the F-box protein FBXO11 in 20 individuals with a variable neurodevelopmental disorder
source.quote: Behavioral abnormalities including autistic features and attention deficits as well as... behavioral problems (17/20), seizures (5/20), cleft lip or palate or bifid uvula (3/20), and minor skeletal anomalies.

evidence.text: In an expanded international cohort of 21 individuals with pathogenic FBXO11 variants, behavioural dysregulation was reported in 62%, alongside hypotonia (62%) and mild intellectual disability (86%).

source.title: Defining FBXO11-Related Neurodevelopmental Disorder
source.quote: Mild intellectual disability (86%), facial dysmorphism (67%), hypotonia (62%), and behavioural dysregulation (62%) were the most prevalent features.

evidence.text: Evaluation of 12 affected individuals from 5 Chinese families with FBXO11 variants revealed core intellectual disability (12/12) and global developmental delay (10/12), but typical hyperactive or aggressive behavioral abnormalities were absent; psychiatric manifestations were limited to hallucinations in only 1 of 12 individuals.

source.title: FBXO11 variants are associated with intellectual disability and variable clinical manifestation in Chinese affected individuals
source.quote: Almost all the affected individuals presented with mild to severe intellectual disability (12/12), global developmental delay (10/12), speech and language development delay (8/12) associated with a range of alternate features including increased body weight (7/12), short stature (6/12), seizures (3/12), reduced visual acuity (4/12), hypotonia (1/12), and auditory hallucinations and hallucinations (1/12). Distinguishingly, malformation was not observed in all the affected individuals.

evidence.text: A familial IDDFBA pedigree involving a mother and two daughters with an inherited truncating FBXO11 variant showed mild intellectual disability and mild dysmorphism without severe hyperactive, aggressive, or autistic behavior.

source.title: The first familial case of inherited intellectual developmental disorder with dysmorphic facies and behavioral abnormalities (IDDFBA) with a novel FBXO11 variant
source.quote: In this family, the mother and two daughters showed mild ID and mild facial dysmorphism.

evidence.text: An assessment of 23 additional individuals with de novo FBXO11 missense variants reinforced that the core universal feature is developmental delay and/or intellectual disability, whereas behavioral anomalies and hypotonia represent variable, non-obligate manifestations.

source.title: De novo missense variants in FBXO11 alter its protein expression and subcellular localization
source.quote: The phenotypic spectrum remains highly variable, with developmental delay and/or intellectual disability as the core feature and behavioral anomalies, hypotonia and various facial dysmorphism as frequent aspects.

conflicts: Cohort penetrance discrepancy: Gregor et al. (2018) documented behavioral abnormalities in 85% (17/20) and preprint data reported 62% (13/21), whereas Pan et al. (2024) observed that in 12 Chinese individuals from 5 families, disruptive behavioral features were not present as a prevailing phenotype, with psychiatric disturbances limited to hallucinations in only 1/12 individuals.

Discriminative utility contradiction: The hypothesis claims behavioral hyperactivity/aggression reliably differentiates IDDFBA from hypoactive or quiet syndromic ID; however, hypotonia is present in up to 62% of cases, and familial cases demonstrate mild ID and dysmorphism without overt hyperactive or aggressive behavioral disruptions.

new_directions.question_text: Does ascertainment bias in initial de novo pediatric cohorts inflate the perceived prevalence of externalizing behavioral abnormalities relative to adult or familial FBXO11 cases?
new_directions.rationale: Initial cohorts prioritized pediatric patients referred specifically for exome sequencing due to severe syndromic ID accompanied by refractory behavioral problems, whereas familial cohorts indicate significantly milder, non-disruptive cognitive presentations.

new_directions.question_text: Do specific missense variants in the CASH or UBR domains correlate with distinct neurobehavioral trajectories compared to protein-truncating loss-of-function variants in FBXO11?
new_directions.rationale: Functional cellular assays demonstrate domain-specific mislocalization patterns (nuclear exclusion vs. cytoplasmic aggregation), which may underlie intra-syndromic phenotypic variation between behavioral dysregulation and purely cognitive presentations.
